explanation: Traffic regulations require every tire in use, including the spare, to keep at least 2 mm of tread depth, since worn tread on any wheel, even one held in reserve for emergency use, reduces road grip and stopping ability.

A vehicle carrying oversize freight that blocks faster traffic must not obstruct following vehicles; the driver is required to ease toward the shoulder and even stop there when needed so others can safely pass.
Aerodynamic drag opposes the vehicle's forward motion and can unbalance it, so wind resistance is primarily a stability and speed factor rather than one affecting brakes or steering wear.

Freight containers are engineered to be secured to a loading platform exclusively through their corner castings using screw anchors (twist locks); other attachment methods do not meet the securing standard.

All twist locks on a container must be engaged before the vehicle moves, because even a few unsecured locks let the container shift or detach under braking or cornering forces, so partial securing is never permitted.

Weight-distribution rules require heavy freight to sit toward the front, between the rear axle and the cab, so the load is properly supported over the axles and does not overload or unbalance the rear of the vehicle.
Sign 226 is the blue instructional sign marking a path reserved for pedestrians, so it is the sign that grants pedestrians permission to enter that route.
Extended, uninterrupted driving is the classic cause of fatigue, and fatigue is dangerous specifically because it can lead to microsleeps or fully falling asleep at the wheel.
Because fatigue cannot be reversed by any driving technique, the only real countermeasure is prevention: sleeping enough before the trip and stopping for genuine rest breaks along the way.
A roadside break only postpones tiredness briefly; it is not a substitute for real rest, so its effect on alertness lasts a short time rather than removing fatigue completely.

Long commercial vehicles have extensive areas around them that the driver cannot see in mirrors or by looking, and their length also limits how sharply they can turn, both of which create extra collision risk.
Two-wheeled vehicles must travel one behind the other rather than side by side; riding level with another motorcycle is allowed only momentarily while completing an overtaking maneuver.
Loose bulk materials may only be loaded up to the height of the truck body's side walls, and any built-in ladders or extensions attached to those walls count toward that height limit.
A safety pin and safety chains are the backup that keeps a trailer attached if the main coupling fails; without them, a coupling failure lets the trailer separate completely from the towing vehicle.
Blind spots are defined as all the zones around the vehicle, not just to the rear, where a road user can be present without the driver being able to detect them by direct sight or through any mirror.
Because the cargo body blocks the driver's rear-facing sightline and mirrors cannot fully compensate, the largest blind zone on a commercial vehicle is directly behind it.
Licensing rules define Class B as covering private cars and commercial vehicles up to a gross weight of 3,500 kg; heavier commercial vehicles or buses require a higher license class.
Since fatigue is only relieved by actual rest, the effective solution when tired is to stop driving and rest, not to compensate by changing speed or using cabin controls.
The pictured sign is the cancellation version of a parking-permission sign, posted where a marked parking zone terminates, so it tells drivers the designated parking area has ended.

Regulations require commercial vehicles above 5,000 kg gross weight to carry two safety shoes (wheel chocks), since heavier vehicles need extra wheel-locking protection when parked, especially on slopes.
Traffic regulations cap the total combined length of a commercial vehicle towing a trailer at 18.75 meters, to keep the combination maneuverable and safe on the road.

Regulations require freight that projects beyond the front of a vehicle to be marked at its tip with a white reflective triangle, so oncoming and other drivers can see the extended edge, especially at night.
A narrow bridge restricts maneuvering space and may only allow one direction of traffic at a time, so a driver must reduce speed both approaching and while crossing it to stay in control.
Because heavy diesel vehicles need extra stopping capability on long descents, regulations require an auxiliary engine/exhaust brake once the vehicle's gross weight exceeds 8,000 kg.

Driving under sedatives is only prohibited when a doctor or the medication's label specifically warns against driving, since some sedatives impair reaction time and alertness enough to make safe driving impossible.
Traffic regulations set the maximum permitted length of a single commercial vehicle, not towing a trailer, at 12 meters, to keep the vehicle stable and maneuverable.

For a loaded commercial vehicle weighing between 3,501 and 8,000 kg, the regulations cap the overall height above the road at 3.50 meters so it can safely clear bridges, tunnels, and overhead obstacles.
On a narrow roadway, a driver confronted by an oncoming vehicle must reduce speed and give way by moving right, even leaving the roadway if that is the only way to avoid a head-on collision.

Regulation 51 requires speed to always be reasonable for the actual road and traffic conditions, and since wet roads reduce tire grip and lengthen braking distance, a reasonable speed on them is necessarily lower than on a dry road.

Braking or accelerating while a vehicle is turning shifts the tires' grip away from cornering, increasing skid risk, so the safe technique is to slow before the curve and hold a steady speed through it.

Regulation 49(a) requires a driver to maintain a gap from the vehicle ahead that leaves room to stop and avoid a collision, which is why keeping a safe distance is the correct rule regardless of grade or road markings.

The distance needed to complete an overtake depends on the relative closing speed between the two vehicles, so both the overtaking vehicle's speed and the overtaken vehicle's speed determine how much distance the maneuver requires.
A commercial vehicle over 2,200 kg is limited by regulation to towing a single vehicle at a time, unless the Licensing Authority has specifically approved towing more.
A strong side wind pushes against the vehicle and can destabilize it, so reducing speed to a level where the driver retains full steering control is the required response.

Sign 216 marks the entrance to an expressway, a road category from which pedestrians, along with animals and slow vehicles, are legally excluded, which is why this sign effectively forbids pedestrian entry.

A vehicle stopped before a pedestrian crossing may be yielding to a pedestrian hidden from the following driver's view, so overtaking it is prohibited to avoid striking a pedestrian who cannot yet be seen.

Once a load's width exceeds 3.40 meters, regulations require an escorting vehicle to accompany the oversize load, since a width beyond this threshold poses a heightened risk to other traffic that needs extra warning.

Freight overhanging the rear of a vehicle must be marked with a red reflective triangle at its tip, since red is the standard rear warning color so following drivers recognize the projecting hazard, especially in low light.

The regulation for marking rearward-projecting freight specifies not only a red reflective triangle but also its exact size, 60 cm per side, so the marker is large enough to be seen clearly from a safe distance.

Regulation 51 defines 'reasonable speed' as one suited to the actual road, traffic, and weather conditions, and this speed can never exceed the posted legal limit even when conditions would otherwise allow faster driving.

Regulations set a maximum service life for towing-vehicle licensing, and once a towing vehicle reaches 19 years from its manufacture date its license may no longer be renewed, reflecting the greater wear of older heavy vehicles.

High beams project a strong, high-angle light that can shine directly into the eyes of oncoming or leading drivers, temporarily impairing their vision, which is the dazzling effect Regulation 99(a) requires drivers to prevent.
Sidewalks are reserved for pedestrians, so bypassing a road obstacle by driving onto one is prohibited regardless of how carefully it is done or how bad the roadway condition is.

Refrigerated, insulated truck bodies are permitted a slightly greater overall width, up to 2.60 meters, than the standard 2.50 meter limit, to account for the extra wall thickness needed for insulation.
The defining legal feature of a trailer is that it has no engine of its own and is built specifically to be towed by a motor vehicle, distinguishing it from a semi-trailer or a motorized towed unit.

A driver who creates a hazard on the roadway by spilling freight is responsible for removing that hazard right away, so the duty is to stop at once and ensure the fallen freight is cleared, not merely to report it.
Sudden braking is generally discouraged because it endangers following traffic, so it is only justified when it is genuinely the sole means available to avoid a collision.

An unpaved dirt road is always treated as the lower-priority road at its junction with a paved road, so a driver exiting onto the paved road must yield to paved-road traffic coming from every direction, not just one side.
Responsibility for a bus's roadworthiness, including having complete first aid equipment on board at all times, rests continuously with the driver, not only at the point the bus leaves the garage.

Because fatigue while driving at night is a genuine danger, the required response is to find a safe spot off the flow of traffic and rest, rather than trying to power through with distractions or stimulants.

A work vehicle is licensed for its specific work function, not as freight or passenger transport, so regulations prohibit carrying freight or passengers anywhere on it apart from seats in the driver's own compartment.
Driving under the influence of alcohol is an absolute prohibition in traffic law, with no exception for amount consumed, occasion, or distance driven.

Regulations permit parking, standing, or stopping only when the vehicle's wheels are within 40 cm of the road's edge, keeping the vehicle close enough to the side to avoid obstructing the traveled lane.

The only reliable way to ensure a safe drive home from a pub is to agree in advance on a designated driver who does not drink at all, since waiting an hour or trusting experience does not reliably remove alcohol's effects.

Reacting to a sudden stop ahead requires enough space to brake within, so maintaining an adequate following distance at all times, rather than relying on watching brake lights, is what actually prevents a rear-end collision.

Sign 146 is a triangular warning sign alerting drivers that wild animals may cross the road ahead, while sign 411 is a prohibitory circular sign that legally bars any animal, led or loose, from entering that road.

Police enforcement authority over load safety includes the power to stop an unlawfully loaded or marked vehicle from continuing until the freight is properly secured or marked, since an unsafe load endangers other road users.

A tire blowout can pull the vehicle suddenly to one side, so keeping a firm grip on the wheel maintains directional control, while gradual, not sudden, braking avoids destabilizing the vehicle further.

Sun glare reduces how far ahead a driver can actually see, so the safe response is to reduce speed to match that reduced visibility and use the sunshade to cut the glare, rather than trying to outrun it.
Reversing is only permitted when a genuine traffic-related need for it exists, since driving backward severely limits the driver's field of view and control compared to driving forward.

The rule for a continuous line paired with a broken line is that only the driver on the broken-line side may cross to overtake; since the continuous line is on your side, you may not cross, while the opposite driver may.
The parking-brake warning light illuminates specifically when the handbrake is engaged, so seeing it lit while driving means the brake is still applying and must be released before continuing.

Being blinded by the sun temporarily reduces how much of the road a driver can see, so the correct response is to slow to a speed matching that reduced sight range rather than trying to drive through it at normal speed.

When an oncoming driver fails to dip their lights, matching them with your own high beam only increases the glare for both drivers, so the safe response is to reduce speed and steer toward the right edge of your lane.
An air braking system that takes longer than normal to build pressure signals a mechanical fault, such as a leak or failing compressor, which requires professional repair rather than a workaround.
A pneumatic braking system's normal operating pressure is a design specification set by the vehicle's manufacturer, since it must match the specific brake hardware installed on that vehicle.
Driving with air pressure below the required minimum is never permitted, because the compressed-air braking system needs a minimum pressure threshold to guarantee full, reliable braking force.

Any modification to a vehicle's design or type requires prior written approval from the Licensing Authority, since unapproved changes could compromise the vehicle's certified safety and roadworthiness.
Sign 146 is the triangular warning sign depicting an animal silhouette that alerts drivers to the possible presence of wild animals crossing the road ahead.

Sign 135 is the advance warning sign posted well before a pedestrian crossing, and it is followed closer to the crossing itself by sign 306, which specifically instructs drivers to give way to pedestrians on that crossing.

A sidecar is legally defined by its structure and attachment, a wheeled fixture fastened to the side of a motorcycle to carry an extra person or cargo, not by speed, spacing, or the motorcycle's own wheel count.
Road marking 804 is the painted line designating a bicycle lane, and cyclists using it are required to travel in the direction the lane's arrow indicates.

A continuous center line prohibits crossing into the opposing lane, so overtaking a slow vehicle ahead is only legal if it can be done entirely within your own lane, without the maneuver requiring you to cross that solid line.
Slow, low-powered vehicles such as tractors are limited to 40 km/h even on inter-urban roads, since their design and braking capability cannot safely handle higher highway speeds.

On urban roads, the general speed limit of 50 km/h applies to small motorcycles up to 125cc/14.6 hp unless a sign specifically states otherwise, the same base limit that applies to cars in built-up areas.
Regulations bar any motor vehicle with three wheels or fewer, which includes motorcycles, from towing another vehicle, since such vehicles lack the stability and structural capacity for safe towing.

Regulation 97(b) requires a motorcycle's headlight and taillight to stay on at all times it is being ridden, day or night, on every type of road, unlike cars which only need lights during designated lighting time.

A vehicle's essential control systems are limited to braking, steering, and acceleration, which are the only inputs that actually change the vehicle's speed and direction; other systems play no role in vehicle control.

When standing on a vehicle-traffic road during dark, unlit conditions, a motorcycle with a sidecar must keep its rear light and parking lights on so other drivers can see the stationary vehicle from a distance.

Before shifting an automatic gearbox out of Park, the vehicle must be held stationary by firmly applying the brakes, since Park alone should not be relied on to prevent unwanted movement during the gear change.

Motorcycle riding is only permitted while wearing an approved helmet that is properly fastened so it cannot come off during riding, since an unsecured helmet gives no real head protection in a fall or collision.

Towing a trailer whose gross weight exceeds 4,000 kg behind a work vehicle requires a combined C+E license class, since this combination exceeds the towing limits covered by a basic work-vehicle or car license.
A motorcyclist must be at least 18 years old before being permitted to carry a passenger, reflecting the added riding skill and judgment needed to safely carry another person.

The legal limit on passengers a motorcycle or sidecar may carry is the number specifically approved by the Licensing Authority and recorded on the vehicle's registration document, not a number set by insurance or seating alone.

A pillion passenger must sit astride the seat with both feet resting on the foot pegs, since this position keeps the passenger balanced and prevents legs from dragging or catching on the road or wheel.
Two-wheeled vehicles are required to ride in single file, and are only permitted to draw level with another two-wheeler momentarily while actually completing an overtaking or bypassing maneuver.
A marked bus station is a no-parking zone for all vehicles, including motorcycles, so parking anywhere within its marked limits is prohibited regardless of how the motorcycle is positioned.

Riding with the kick-stand still extended risks the stand striking the road surface, especially while leaning into a turn, which can catch and throw the motorcycle off balance and cause it to roll over.

The overriding safety principle for carrying anything on a motorcycle is that it must never interfere with the rider's ability to fully control the machine, since loss of control is what actually causes a crash.

New tractor-license holders must wait 6 months of experience before being permitted to drive a heavier tractor or one towing a trailer over 4,000 kg, giving them time to build basic handling skill first.

Under Israel's graduated motorcycle licensing, the entry-level Class A2 covers the smallest motorcycles, 125cc or less with power up to 14.6 hp (11 kW), which is why this power range requires an A2 license.
The next tier up in Israel's graduated motorcycle licensing, Class A1, covers motorcycles with power up to 33 hp (25 kW), sitting between the entry-level A2 class and the unrestricted A class.
Once a motorcycle's engine power exceeds 33 hp (25 kW), it falls outside the limits of both the A2 and A1 classes, requiring the unrestricted Class A license.
Class A2, the entry-level motorcycle license, can be obtained at age 16, but because the applicant is a minor, the law requires the written consent of a parent or guardian.
The law requires a pillion passenger to keep both feet on the foot supports throughout the ride, since this keeps the passenger's weight balanced and their legs clear of the wheels and road.

Unlike a car's single brake pedal that applies all wheel brakes together, a motorcycle has independent controls, a hand lever for the front brake and a foot pedal for the rear, letting the rider operate each separately.

A reasonable and safe riding speed, consistent with the general reasonable-speed principle, is one slow enough that the rider can perceive every relevant road detail and still keep full control of the motorcycle.

When visibility is impaired, both the driver's sight distance and reaction margin shrink, so the correct response is to reduce speed and increase the following gap, giving more time and space to react to hazards.

A wide field of view through the helmet lets a rider take in more of the surrounding road environment, which is what allows them to judge a safe following distance and speed, and notice hazards sooner, shortening response time.

Braking, swerving, and accelerating are all ultimately limited by how much traction the tires have with the road surface, since every one of those actions depends on the tires transmitting force to the ground without sliding.
